bib.title: Introduction to Information Retrieval, Chapter 15: Support vector machines and machine learning on documents
bib.venue: Cambridge University Press (online edition, draft of April 1, 2009)

question: How do large-margin classifiers (SVMs) work for text, how should one choose and improve a text classifier in practice, and how can the same learning machinery rank documents in ad hoc retrieval?
contributions: Derivation of hard-margin, soft-margin, multiclass and kernel SVMs (15.1-15.2)
Practical guidance on choosing a text classifier by training-data size and engineering features (15.3)
Machine-learned scoring and the ranking SVM for ad hoc retrieval (15.4)

limits: Written 2008-09: pre-deep-learning. Neural networks are listed once in the intro; no word embeddings, transformers, dense retrieval or neural rerankers.

Learning to rank is presented as 'too early to write something definitive'; it covers only linear pointwise/pairwise models (ranking SVM). No listwise methods, LambdaMART, or gradient-boosted rankers beyond reference pointers.

The only experimental table (15.2) is reported from Joachims 2002a, uses break-even F1 which the authors say many researchers disprefer, and Reuters-21578 only; no seeds, variances or significance tests.
The chapter itself says results for the same method differ between papers (Naive Bayes in Joachims 1998 looks too weak).
Complexity figures (O(|D|^1.7), cutting planes) are from 2006 solvers; no GPU or stochastic-gradient SVM training such as Pegasos/liblinear is discussed.
The kernel section gives no guidance on choosing sigma or d; the chapter claims 90% of kernel work uses polynomial or rbf kernels with no source.
Ranking SVM claim of outperforming hand-built rankers has no number in the chapter.
practices: With no labelled data and domain experts available, start with hand-written Boolean standing queries (15.3.1, p. 335).
With little labelled data, prefer a high-bias classifier such as Naive Bayes; avoid kNN; consider semi-supervised or transductive SVMs, or get more labels (15.3.1, p. 336).
Get labels by embedding labelling in users' natural tasks; consider active learning (15.3.1, p. 336).
Overlay a Boolean rule layer on a linear classifier such as an SVM so individual documents can be fixed quickly (15.3.1, pp. 336-337).
With huge data, choose the classifier on scalability and runtime efficiency, since the choice matters little (15.3.1, p. 337).
Try a linear SVM with default C=1 first; with soft margins it beat polynomial and rbf kernels on Reuters (15.2.4 fn 5, p. 334).
If a quadratic kernel is wanted only for word-pair conjunctions, consider materialising the features and training a linear SVM (15.2.1, pp. 329-330).
Use one-versus-rest for multiclass SVMs, choosing the class with greatest margin (15.2.2, p. 330).
Return 'don't know' inside the margin or below a confidence threshold, and fit a sigmoid (Platt 2000) to turn scores into probabilities (15.1, p. 325).
Engineer features: collapse years, ISBNs and similar tokens by regex, add character k-grams and discriminative multiword patterns (15.3.2, pp. 338-339).
Upweight title words (about 2x) and tie parameters across zones rather than separate per-zone feature spaces (15.3.2, pp. 339-340).
Do not expect stemming to help classification when data are plentiful; aggressive stemming can hurt (15.3.2, p. 339).
Combine classifiers with voting, bagging or boosting for a small boost, and send low-confidence decisions to manual review (15.3.2, p. 338).
Treat ranking as ordinal regression and train on pairwise feature differences rather than on absolute relevance labels (15.4.2, pp. 344-345).
Hand-engineer nonlinear transforms (log tf, idf) of features, because learners only find weights for linear combinations (15.4.2, pp. 345-346).

terms.definition: This distance from the decision surface to the closest data point determines the margin of the classifier.
the (usually small) subset of the data which defines the position of the separator
y_i(w^T x_i + b); of a data set, twice the minimal functional margin of any point
the maximum width of the band that can be drawn separating the support vectors of the two classes; rho = 2/|w|
xi_i; a non-zero value allows x_i to not meet the margin requirement at a cost proportional to xi_i
a regularization term which controls overfitting: large C respects the data at the cost of margin, small C allows a fat margin that models the bulk of the data
a function K that corresponds to a dot product in some expanded feature space
a kernel satisfying Mercer's condition: continuous, symmetric, with positive definite gram matrix
generalisation where classes are arbitrary structured objects with relationships between them
the specialised field between classification and regression where a ranking is predicted
an SVM trained on feature-difference vectors of document pairs for the same query, requiring w^T Phi(d_i,d_j,q) >= 1 - xi when d_i precedes d_j
using the same features and parameters across document zones while weighting occurrences by zone
designing additional features suited to a specific problem; remains a human craft

problems: Chapter is the online edition draft (c) 2009 dated April 1, 2009; book edition is 2008.

Equations and Table 15.2/15.3 are flattened by extraction; Table 15.2 column order (NB, Rocchio, Dec. Trees, kNN, linear SVM C=0.5, C=1.0, rbf-SVM) was inferred from the header sequence and the stated microavg result.
Eq 15.12 prints w = sum alpha y_i x_i with alpha lacking subscript (possible typo or extraction loss).
Example 15.1 text states constraint as 'sign(yi(w^T x_i + b)) >= 1', which is loose notation.
Example 15.1 gives two forms of the same hyperplane (weight (1,2), b=-5.5 vs (2/5,4/5), b=-11/5); they agree up to scaling, not an error.
Figure 15.1 text says 5 support vectors; the figure itself is not checked from text.
